newsitem.title: USA: April U.S. vehicle sales seen held back by strikes.
newsitem.headline: April U.S. vehicle sales seen held back by strikes.

text.p: Strikes at Chrysler Corp and General Motors Corp contributed to softer U.S. retail car and truck sales in April, but the walkouts will probably take a bigger bite out of May sales, analysts said on Tuesday.

Chrysler dealers in April sold down their inventories of Jeep Grand Cherokee sport utility vehicles and Dodge Ram and Dakota pickup trucks, the vehicles most affected by a 19-day strike at the automaker's Mound Road engine plant in Detroit.

Together, the Chrysler strike and walkouts at two GM plants reduced industry sales for April by about 25,000 to 30,000 vehicles, said Chris Cedergren, an automotive consultant with Nextrend Inc in Thousand Oaks, Calif.
"We're seeing the beginnings of the strike effect on sales," Cedergren said. "The real impact is going to be in the month of May, especially if the strikes continue into the middle of the month."
He estimated May sales could decline by more than 100,000 units if the strikes extend into the second half of the month.

Analysts surveyed by Reuters expect automakers to report April U.S. car and light-truck sales at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 14.7 million to 15 million units, well below the March pace of 15.8 million. The April 1996 sales rate was about 15.1 million.
GM and Chrysler are expected to report results on Thursday, while Ford Motor Co will release its sales on Monday, May 5.

Burnham Securities analyst David Healy said he expected Chrysler truck sales to be little changed from year-ago levels at 139,800, despite the halt in production of Chrysler's most popular truck models. He forecast a 13 percent drop in Chrysler's passenger car sales.

The week-old strike at GM's Pontiac, Mich., truck plant has curtailed production of the automaker's popular full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickups, but GM truck sales are expected to come in about at about the same level as a year earlier.

Analysts expect GM's car sales to suffer an eight percent decline, in part because a 25-day strike at GM's Oklahoma City car plant has held back the production launch of the new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-size sedans.
GM's car sales comparisons also were expected to suffer from slow launches of other cars and heavy sales to rental fleets in the year-ago period.
"At this point, it appears that April's sales softness represents a pause from the first quarter's unsustainable sales pace rather than a significant decline," Healy said.

Market share gains by Japanese automakers are expected to moderate in April, in part because inventories of many popular models, such as Toyota Motor Corp's new Camry, have been depleted by spring sales promotions. The Camry was the best-selling car in the United States in the first quarter.
"The demand for the Camry is at unprecedented levels," Cedergren said. "If they had more volume, they could sell it."
Demand by Americans for German-made cars also remains strong, with Mercedes-Benz, Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG and Volkswagen AG expected to post robust gains over year-ago sales.
